summary: Defines the SPPI, the adapted subset of SNMP's Structure of Management Information used to write Policy Information Base modules. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: It is the grammar for writing rule books for network machines. It's old now.

subtitle: The grammar for writing rule books that define how network devices behave.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a way to centrally define and push policies to devices (like rate limits or security rules) without configuring each device individually. The policy definitions must be formal enough for tools to parse and enforce them.
tldr.mechanism: SPPI defines an ASN.1-based language modeled on SNMP's SMI to write Policy Information Base (PIB) modules. A PIB module defines Provisioning Classes (PRCs) and their attributes, which servers create and send to devices via the COPS-PR protocol to control behavior.
tldr.outcome: Operators can define policies once and deploy them uniformly across devices. SPPI is now Historic because other policy distribution approaches (like NETCONF with YANG models) have become preferred, but it remains important for understanding policy-based networking history.

today: RFC 3159 is Historic. Policy-based networking as defined by SPPI and COPS-PR has largely been replaced by Software-Defined Networking (SDN), intent-based networking, and direct device configuration using NETCONF and YANG models. However, legacy systems may still use SPPI-based policy modules, and understanding SPPI remains valuable for network management history and for operators working with older infrastructure.

sections.title: Policy Provisioning: Pushing Rules from Center to Edge
sections.content:
In the early 2000s, network operators wanted to manage policies centrally: bandwidth limits, QoS rules, security filters, and other behaviors. Instead of logging into each router or switch individually, they wanted a policy server (a Policy Decision Point, or PDP) to define policies once and push them to network devices (Policy Enforcement Points, or PEPs). The COPS-PR protocol provided the network transport for this, but something was needed to formally describe what policies look like so both the server and the devices could agree on the structure.

SPPI (Structure of Policy Provisioning Information) solved that by providing a formal language and data model, based on SNMP's successful Structure of Management Information (SMI), to define Policy Information Base (PIB) modules that describe policies.
sections.plainLanguage: Before SPPI, telling every router 'block traffic from X to Y' meant logging in to each one and typing commands. With SPPI, a policy server could say to all routers at once, following a standard format, 'here is a rule.' The routers would understand because they all speak the same grammar.

sections.title: Provisioning Classes, Instances, and Attributes
sections.content:
SPPI borrows terminology from SNMP but adapts it for policy. Where SNMP talks about 'managed objects,' SPPI uses Provisioning Classes (PRCs), which are templates like 'QoS rate limit rule' or 'access control entry.' Each actual rule is a Provisioning Instance (PRI)—one instance of a rate limit rule applied to a specific user. The properties of a rule (like the limit rate or the user ID) are called attributes.

A PIB module is a collection of related PRCs and their definitions, written in ASN.1 syntax. Modules can be imported into other modules for reuse, just as MIB modules work. PRCs use concepts like PIB-INDEX (to identify instances), AUGMENTS (to extend one PRC with additional attributes), and PIB-REFERENCES (to link rules to other rules or resources).
sections.plainLanguage: A PRC is a template (like 'player on a team'). A PRI is one actual player (like 'Alice, jersey 10'). Attributes are properties (Alice's position, her stats). A PIB module is the rulebook that says what attributes each player must have.

sections.title: Data Types and Syntax
sections.content:
SPPI defines a set of base data types for attributes. In addition to basic types like INTEGER and OCTET STRING inherited from SMI, SPPI adds Integer64 and Unsigned64 to handle larger numbers. Attributes can have restricted values (like enumerations) and textual conventions—reusable type definitions with specific semantics (for example, 'bandwidth in kilobits per second').

SPPI also defines special textual conventions for policy work: InstanceId (to identify a PRI uniquely), ReferenceId (to point to another PRI), Prid (a full path to a PRI as an OID), TagId (to group related instances), and TagReferenceId (to reference a group). These allow complex policy structures where rules reference other rules, queues, or user groups.
sections.plainLanguage: SPPI defines the types of information in rules: numbers, text, lists of choices, and pointers to other rules. If a rule says 'apply this rate limit to all traffic tagged with ID 5,' the ID is a TagId and the rate limit is a reference to another rule.

sections.title: Writing a PIB Module
sections.content:
A PIB module starts with a MODULE-IDENTITY clause that declares the module's name, organization, contact, and description. It includes a SUBJECT-CATEGORIES clause that indicates which COPS Client Types (like 'QoS' or 'access control') the module applies to.

For each PRC, a module defines two OBJECT-TYPE macros: a table definition (the collection of all instances) and a row definition (one instance). The row definition's SYNTAX is a SEQUENCE of attributes. Each attribute is also an OBJECT-TYPE with a PIB-ACCESS clause ('install' if the PDP can install it, 'notify' if the PEP reports it, 'install-notify' for both, or 'report-only' if it is read-only).

PIB modules also include OBJECT-GROUP and MODULE-COMPLIANCE macros to specify which attributes and groups are mandatory for implementations, maintaining interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: A PIB module is like a book chapter. It has a title (MODULE-IDENTITY), describes its scope (SUBJECT-CATEGORIES), and lists the types of rules (PRCs) with all the fields (attributes) each rule must have.

sections.title: Deployment and Why SPPI Became Historic
sections.content:
SPPI was standardized in 2001 for use with the COPS-PR protocol and policy-based networking. Real-world deployments used it to manage QoS policies (via PIB modules for DiffServ and bandwidth management), access control lists, and RSVP reservation policies. However, SPPI and COPS-PR had limitations: COPS was a separate protocol not integrated with mainstream network management, and SPPI's ASN.1 syntax was less accessible to modern engineers than YANG.

By the 2010s, operators increasingly moved toward YANG models with NETCONF for configuration, which provides a more flexible and web-friendly approach. SPPI was classified as Historic because the policy-based networking model it served has largely been superseded by SDN, direct device configuration, and intent-based networking models. Nevertheless, understanding SPPI remains important for anyone working with legacy policy systems or studying the history of centralized network management.
sections.plainLanguage: SPPI worked well for its time, like a paper forms system. But when email and web forms became standard, paper forms became old-fashioned. SPPI became historic not because it was wrong, but because better tools appeared.
